title: Three-Property Rule Strategy
name: Three-Property Rule Strategy
metaTitle: Three-Property Rule Strategy in San Diego, CA
metaDescription: Three-property rule strategy in San Diego weighs a tight three-name list against the 200 percent alternative given the market's high per-unit pricing.

sections.html:
The three-property rule sounds like the simple option: name up to three replacement properties of any value and move forward. In a San Diego market where a single well-located multifamily or medical office building can represent most of an exchanger's proceeds, simple doesn't always mean sufficient, and picking this rule over the alternatives deserves more thought than the name suggests.

Plenty of San Diego exchangers pick the three-property rule by default because a broker mentioned it first, not because anyone actually compared it against the 200% and 95% alternatives for the specific exchange in front of them.

sections.heading: How the Rule Actually Works
sections.html: Under the three-property rule, an exchanger can identify up to three replacement properties within the 45-day window regardless of their combined value, and there's no requirement to acquire all three — only enough to satisfy the exchange's value and debt-replacement needs. This is the rule most exchangers default to because it's the easiest to explain, but defaulting to it without comparing it against the 200% and 95% alternatives can leave less flexibility than a San Diego search actually needs.

sections.heading: Where Three Names Isn't Enough in This Market
sections.html: San Diego's tighter asset classes — medical office near the coast, well-positioned multifamily, single-tenant retail in visitor corridors — move fast enough, and price high enough per property, that naming only three candidates can leave an exchanger with no real backup if financing or diligence falls through on the top choice. A buyer working with a mid-size exchange value might find that three properties in this market represent a much larger share of total proceeds than three properties would in a market with lower per-unit pricing, which raises the cost of a single deal falling apart.

sections.heading: When the Three-Property Rule Is Actually the Right Call
sections.html:
Run through this comparison before defaulting to any single identification rule, since the right choice depends on the shape of the exchange, not habit.

  • Exchange value modest enough that three well-vetted properties genuinely cover the likely acquisition need
  • A short list already narrowed through prior sourcing, rather than three names picked to fill out the count
  • Strong confidence in financing on the top choice, reducing the need for backup candidates
  • A single asset class search, such as one self-storage facility, where three genuine candidates are realistic to find
  • Comfort walking away from the exchange entirely if all three fall through, since the rule doesn't allow adding a fourth after day forty-five

sections.heading: The 200% Rule as the More Common San Diego Fit
sections.html:
For exchangers who want real backup options without being boxed into three names, the 200% rule allows identifying more properties as long as their combined fair market value doesn't exceed twice the relinquished property's sale price. Given San Diego per-unit pricing, this rule often produces a more realistic identification list — five or six candidates across a couple of submarkets — without requiring the exchanger to guess correctly on the first three names.

That said, more names on a list isn't automatically better, since each additional candidate still needs real due diligence before the deadline, and a long list assembled in a hurry to satisfy the 200% math can end up thinner on verification than a short list of three properties that were actually vetted properly.

sections.heading: Getting the Choice Locked In With the Qualified Intermediary
sections.html:
Decide which identification rule fits the exchange before building the candidate list, not after, since switching approaches midway through the 45-day window wastes time that should go toward vetting actual properties. Confirm the choice and the resulting list with the qualified intermediary in writing well before the deadline, and review the debt and value math with a tax advisor if the exchange involves multiple properties or mixed asset classes.

Revisit the choice again once real offers are on the table, since a rule selected early in the search based on rough assumptions about San Diego pricing may need adjusting once actual candidate values come back from appraisal or broker opinion.

faqs.q: How many properties can I identify under the three-property rule?
faqs.a: Up to three replacement properties, of any combined value, within the 45-day identification window. There's no requirement to acquire all three, only enough to satisfy the exchange's value and debt-replacement needs.

faqs.q: Why might three properties not be enough in a San Diego exchange?
faqs.a: San Diego's per-unit pricing in tighter asset classes can make three candidates represent a large share of total exchange proceeds, so losing one to financing or diligence issues leaves less room to recover. The 200% rule can provide more realistic backup options in that situation.

faqs.q: When does the three-property rule make the most sense?
faqs.a: It fits best when the exchange value is modest relative to San Diego pricing, the candidate list is already well vetted, and financing confidence on the top choice is strong. It's a weaker fit when an exchanger needs real backup options across multiple properties.

faqs.q: Can I switch from the three-property rule to the 200% rule after starting my search?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as any change to the identification list happens before the 45-day window closes. Deciding on the right rule early avoids wasting search time on a list structured for the wrong approach.

faqs.q: Does choosing an identification rule affect financing or tax outcomes?
faqs.a: The rule itself governs identification mechanics, but the resulting property list affects financing timelines and, if multiple properties are involved, basis and boot calculations. Review the full picture with a tax advisor when the exchange involves more than one replacement property.
